title: Import formalities, customs clearance & release
sceneDesc: Four illustrated stations show what must happen before the container can leave the port: arrival notice, import declaration, Bill of Lading and payment, and release with a pick-up code.

flow.strip: Import demurrage free time: {freeDays} days from discharge (illustrative)

narration.1: The customer received my arrival notice. Now two 'yes' are needed: one from customs, one from the carrier.
narration.2: Import starts with the arrival notice: charges, free time and release conditions. Two releases are needed — customs (legal) and carrier (commercial). [TO VERIFY:v66]
narration.3: Release = customs release + carrier release (transport document, payment, holds) + terminal release (PIN or digital pick-up right). Any one missing blocks the gate-out. [TO VERIFY:v68]

narration.1: A customs broker declares me to {importCustoms}: what's inside, its value and its origin. The importer pays duties and taxes.
narration.2: The [[import-declaration]] (HS code, customs value, origin, preferential proofs) is lodged by the importer's broker; duties and import VAT are paid or deferred; [[eori]] required in the EU. [TO VERIFY:v67]
narration.3: Customs value, classification and origin drive duties; risk-based selection may add a scan or physical exam. Under DDP the seller is the importer — check EU representation. [TO VERIFY:v26] [TO VERIFY:v67]

caption.2: Under {incoterm}, import clearance is done by the {importBy}.

narration.1: The customer gives the carrier an original Bill of Lading and pays what's due. It's like showing my ticket to pick up my luggage.
narration.2: For a 'to order' B/L, the bank [[endorsement|endorses]] an original to the consignee, who surrenders it to the carrier with payment of collect freight and charges. Sea waybill or express release: no original needed. [TO VERIFY:v68]
narration.3: The carrier checks the endorsement chain and that the presenter is the lawful holder; one original surrendered accomplishes the set. Delivery without original = misdelivery exposure. [TO VERIFY:v75]

narration.1: Customs says yes, the carrier says yes: I'm released! The terminal gets the message and a secret pick-up code is given to the truck company.
narration.2: Customs release and carrier release reach the terminal (often via a port community system); the haulier gets a [[pin]] or digital pick-up right and books a slot. [TO VERIFY:v68]
narration.3: Release data must match the collecting haulier; PIN security matters — cargo theft by fraudulent pick-up is a known risk, hence secure digital pick-up schemes. [TO VERIFY:v68]
The originals are stuck at the buyer's bank because of an L/C discrepancy. Demurrage is running. The consignee asks you to release the box against a letter of indemnity ([[loi]]).

text.1: Three original Bills of Lading are usually issued, but presenting just one is enough to collect the goods — the others then become void.
text.2: Delivering cargo without the original B/L is one of the most common causes of large claims against carriers. [TO VERIFY:v75]

body.1: Customs checks what I carry, collects duties and taxes, and makes sure nothing forbidden enters. Under {incoterm}, the {importBy} handles import customs.

body.2: Lodged by the importer or its broker with HS code, customs value, origin and supporting documents (invoice, packing list, certificate of origin). Duties and import VAT paid or deferred. [TO VERIFY:v67]
body.3: Wrong classification or value → penalties and post-clearance audits; preferential origin needs valid proofs. Under DDP, the seller is the importer of record. [TO VERIFY:v26]

body.1: The carrier lets me go only when it has the right paper (or electronic release) and the charges are paid.

body.2: With a [[sea-waybill]], the named consignee gets the cargo without an original. With [[telex-release|express release]], originals were surrendered at origin. eB/Ls transfer electronically. [TO VERIFY:v49]

2.explain: A 'to order of [bank]' B/L is transferred by the bank's endorsement, typically once the importer has paid or accepted under the L/C.

3.prompt: One line makes this original unacceptable for release. Tap it.
3.explain: The importer endorsed the B/L to itself: only the bank, named on the front, can endorse it. Releasing on this original would expose the carrier to the bank's claim. [TO VERIFY:v75]

1.2: The terminal checks the pick-up right before releasing the box; in some ports secure digital systems replace PIN codes. [TO VERIFY:v68]

2.2: Without customs release, the box stays — even if the carrier has released it. [TO VERIFY:v67]

3.2: After demurrage free time, daily charges apply until gate-out; then import detention runs until the empty is returned. [TO VERIFY:v21]

2.prompt: What does the haulier need at the terminal gate to collect the box?

options.text: The valid pick-up right (PIN or digital token), with customs release on the box and a slot if required
The arrival notice
options.fb: That's information for the consignee, not a pick-up right.

options.text: The original B/L
options.fb: The B/L goes to the carrier, not to the gate.

options.text: The VGM

2.explain: The gate releases against the pick-up right and status flags (customs, carrier). [TO VERIFY:v68]

3.prompt: The PIN was e-mailed to three haulage companies 'to be safe'. A truck nobody ordered collects the box. What went wrong?

options.text: PIN security: pick-up rights must go only to the appointed haulier, ideally via secure digital release
Nothing — any truck with the PIN is legitimate
options.fb: The PIN proves knowledge of a code, not authority.

options.text: Customs released too early
options.fb: Customs release isn't the issue here.

options.text: The B/L wasn't endorsed
options.fb: The documents were fine; the pick-up right leaked.

3.explain: Fraudulent pick-ups exploit shared codes; ports have introduced secure digital pick-up for this reason. [TO VERIFY:v68]

documents: **Original B/L** (endorsed), or sea waybill / express release / eB/L. [TO VERIFY:v68]
**Release / delivery order** with PIN or digital pick-up right.
costs: **Duties and import VAT** — for the importer (the seller under DDP). [TO VERIFY:v26]
**Collect freight, destination THC, documentation fee**. [TO VERIFY:v35]
**Demurrage** if release takes too long. [TO VERIFY:v21]
jobs: **Import documentation / release desk** — B/L checks, releases.
**Finance / credit control** — collect freight and charges.
**Legal / claims** — LOI policy, misdelivery claims. [TO VERIFY:v75]

incoNote.DDP: Under DDP, the seller clears import and pays duties and VAT — it must be able to act as importer. [TO VERIFY:v26]
incoNote.*: Under {incoterm}, import clearance, duties and taxes are for the buyer.

1: Customs must clear me and the importer pays duties and taxes.
The carrier releases me against an original Bill of Lading (or an electronic release) and payment.
Then the truck company gets a pick-up code.
2: Two releases: customs (legal) and carrier (commercial); both reach the terminal.
A 'to order' B/L needs the right endorsement; waybills and express releases avoid paper originals.
Pick-up rights (PIN, digital) must be protected.
3: Never release without the lawful original unless the LOI policy is applied and approved.
Check endorsement chains — the named party endorses.
Release fraud is real: use secure pick-up processes.

1.hint: I'm still in the port. The customer's warehouse is inland.

options.text: A truck (or a train or a barge) takes me from the port to the customer.
options.confirm: Yes! That's the on-carriage. Under {incoterm}, it's organised by {onBy}.

options.text: The customer unloads me inside the port.
options.why: Full containers usually travel to the customer's premises to be unloaded.
options.realLife: Terminals don't let customers unload boxes on the quay.
options.whenRight: LCL or port-side warehouses (CFS) — a different service.

options.text: I go back to {pol} first.
options.why: My cargo is for this customer — I don't need to go back.
options.realLife: That would cost a fortune and take weeks.

2.prompt: Customs and carrier releases have reached the terminal. What happens next?

options.text: On-carriage: the appointed haulier collects the box with the pick-up right; a gate-out EIR is issued; import detention starts.
options.confirm: Correct. Gate-out ends demurrage; import detention runs until the empty is returned. Under {incoterm}, on-carriage is organised by {onBy}. [TO VERIFY:v21]

options.text: The consignee unstuffs the box at the terminal.
options.why: FCL boxes are unstuffed at the consignee's premises.
options.realLife: Terminals don't offer that for FCL, except via a CFS service.

options.text: The box must first return to the origin depot.
options.why: The box delivers its cargo first; the empty is returned at destination.

options.text: Customs escorts the box to the consignee.
options.why: Released goods move freely; escorts are exceptional.
options.realLife: Only for specific procedures (e.g. some transit or high-risk goods).

3.prompt: Case: originals stuck at the bank; demurrage running; the consignee asks for release against an LOI. What do you do?

options.text: Apply the company's LOI policy: usually decline, or accept only with a bank-countersigned LOI approved by legal; meanwhile inform the consignee that demurrage continues.
options.confirm: Right. Releasing without the original exposes the carrier to the lawful holder (here possibly the bank). A countersigned LOI reduces but doesn't remove the risk. [TO VERIFY:v75]

options.text: Release immediately: the consignee is a good customer.
options.why: The original holder may still claim the goods.
options.realLife: Misdelivery claims can equal the full cargo value.

options.text: Release against a copy of the B/L.
options.realLife: Same exposure as releasing without anything.

options.text: Stop the demurrage clock until the bank releases the originals.
options.why: Bank delays are a cargo-side matter under most tariffs.
options.whenRight: Only if agreed commercially and documented.
